newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk forces, rebels keep up month-old fight in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turk forces, rebels keep up month-old fight in Iraq.

text.p: Turkish forces and their Iraqi Kurdish allies clashed off and on with separatist rebels in a month-old incursion into northern Iraq, but there were signs on Friday of Turkish firepower being withdrawn from the region.

Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas fought with Turkish soldiers in and around the Zap region, from where the PKK has in the past used bases to launch attacks into southeast Turkey, sources close to the rebels said.
On the Turkish-Iraqi border, 11 Turkish tanks returned to Turkey from northern Iraq on Friday through the Habur border gate, witnesses said.
In Turkey, Kurdish guerrillas opened fire with automatic weapons on a village in the eastern province of Elazig late on Thursday, killing one villager and wounding two, security sources said.
Two soldiers, on the way to the village after the attack, were also wounded by a land-mine explosion, they said.
Two people were wounded in a separate rocket attack on a village in Diyarbakir province, the sources said.
Empty Turkish military trucks and buses entered northern Iraq on Thursday, but there was no confirmation of a troop withdrawal from the region.
More than 10,000 Turkish troops streamed into northern Iraq on May 14 in pursuit of PKK rebels, who have fought the military since 1984 for self-rule in southeast Turkey.
The Turkish military says it has killed around 2,500 rebels for the loss of about 100 soldiers since the operation started, while the PKK says it has killed around 800 soldiers.
The operation, carried out under a strict news blackout, has drawn criticism from NATO member Turkey's Western allies and countries in the Middle East.

The Arab League secretariat has condemned the incursion, calling for the withdrawal of troops from the so-called Kurdish "safe haven", set up after the Gulf War in 1991 to protect the local population from attacks by Baghdad.

Pro-Kurdish MED-TV said on Friday Turkish forces had abandoned the strategic Betrut hill, which they were using as a base to establish control over the Zap region, after an attack by PKK rebels early on Thursday.

In the Zap region, the rebels killed seven Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) fighters, who are backing Turkey's bid to force the PKK guerrillas from the region, in an attack at Kurajaru on Thursday night, a MED-TV spokesman told Reuters.
He said the guerrillas clashed further with KDP militiamen in the Hakurk region on the Iraq-Iran border.
Opposition Iraqi sources said earlier this week there was a big battle between the PKK and KDP near Haji Homaran, where the colonial-era Hamilton Road crosses from Iraq into Iran.
They said the PKK had been joined in its fight by the Kurdish Hizbollah, the Kurdistan Conservative Party and the Kurdistan Social Democratic Party -- all believed to have close ties to Iran.

The KDP, the main power in northern Iraq, had sent two corps of 2,000 peshmerga guerrillas each to the area to combat between 700 to 1,000 PKK guerrillas, said to have entered from Iran armed with Soviet-designed Grad multiple missile launchers.
Turkey has blamed Iran, Syria and other countries for providing the PKK with sophisticated weaponry, including shoulder-fired SA-7 missiles used to shoot down two Turkish helicopters.
Early on Friday, the rebels launched an attack with rocket-propelled grenades near the village of Kasrok, killing eight soldiers, MED-TV said.
